question: The background picture in Oil Ocean fills the console's background picture memory completely, right up to a hardware wall, so the parallax editor cannot add a single new moving band to it. Not even the smallest one. The wall is real and cannot be moved: the background tiles end exactly where the sprite table begins, and every last slot is holding a distinct piece of artwork with no duplicates, no blank tiles and no mirrored pairs left to reclaim. The tool that drew the current background was never told to leave any room, so it used all of it. The version of that tool used before it deliberately kept about a hundred slots back for animation, and that reservation is what got lost. Whether the background art gets redrawn to make room is an art call, and it is yours.

options.name: Animate background artwork that is already there
options.what: Parts of the background that are already drawn can be turned into moving bands. This works on the real level today and needs no picture memory at all, because nothing new is drawn. What you cannot do is add a new moving element, or move artwork somewhere it is not already sitting. The four empty band slots stay empty.
options.costs: No art work and no waiting. One check is still outstanding on my side: the end to end path has been proven with a band built by the code, not yet with one built by hand in the editor. That check is a queue item and about an hour.

options.name: Redraw the background with room kept back for animation
options.what: The art tool gets told to stop short of the wall and keep slots free. Every band slot then becomes usable for anything you want to put in it, and the two animated bands that the last art run wiped out can come back at the same time.
options.costs: The background picture loses roughly a quarter of its distinct detail, which is a thing you would see if you stopped and looked at the sky and the rig. It costs one art run plus your eyes on the result, and it is work on the engine side rather than mine.

recommend.because: It puts a moving background on screen without touching art you already approved, and it is the only one of the two that can start today. If you later decide to redraw and keep room back, adding bands from scratch starts working on its own and none of the work built so far is wasted. So this is not a road that has to be undone, it is the first half of the same road.

detail: aeon games/sonic4/data/editor_bg_override.json is at 448/448 tiles. tileSlotsRemaining 0, bandsRemaining 4. 448 = (0xB800-0x8000)/32 exactly; the SAT at $B800 is the wall, tile 449 sprays into it. Measured against aeon pin e087af9c: 448 distinct bitmaps, 0 flip-redundant pairs over orig/H/V/HV, 0 uniform-colour, no H- or V-symmetric tiles, so dedup/blank/flip reclaim are all exhausted. The lever is the generator, not dedup: png_to_bg_override.py has no --max-tiles and only refuses above the ceiling; the superseded forest_bg_gen.py reserved 108 tiles by construction. Current blob is the output of the run that destroyed the two authored bands (see ROADMAP items 14 and 24). insertBand refuses at every size under saturation; promote/demote leave tiles.length unchanged and function today (item 27). The outstanding UI-made-band composition check is item 29.

question: The editor is showing you a different background from the one the game actually uses, and that is why the new band-motion preview refuses to run on your real project. The picture on the map canvas comes from Aurora's background library; the background the ROM is built from comes from editor_bg_override.json. They hold the same artwork at completely different tile numbers (0 of 320 tiles line up by position, though all 320 appear somewhere in the other). Nothing in either program has ever connected the two. Which one should win?

options.what: The map canvas reads editor_bg_override.json when one exists, so what you see is what the game builds. The band preview then works on the real project instead of refusing, and item 43 (drawing bands directly on the preview) becomes possible on real data.
options.costs: The map will look different the first time you open it — you will see the regenerated 320-tile background you approved in d-10 instead of the older 448-tile one it shows today. The background library becomes display-only for any section that has an override, so editing background art through the library stops changing what you see until that edit reaches the override.

options.name: Keep the library picture, and rebuild the ROM background from it
options.what: editor_bg_override.json gets regenerated from the background you currently see, so the game matches the editor.
options.costs: This throws away the regeneration you approved in d-10 — the one that freed 128 tiles specifically so bands would fit — and it undoes itself: adding or removing a band renumbers the override by design (that is the prefix rule), so the two would drift apart again the moment you author anything.

options.name: Leave them separate
options.what: Nothing changes. The preview keeps refusing on the real project and explains why on screen.
options.costs: The feature you asked for does not work where you would use it, and the editor keeps showing you a background the game does not use — which is a trap independent of the preview.

recommend.because: editor_bg_override.json is the ONLY thing the ROM bakes for this background — aeon's inject_editor_bg.py reads it and writes the generated zone_bg.bin/bg_tiles.bin, and I checked that no aeon tool reads the background library at all. So the override is already the truth about what ships; the library is a picture we show you. The second option is self-undoing for the reason in its cost line, and the third leaves a background on screen that the game will not use, which will mislead somebody eventually.
